papers.abstract: Embodied foundation models hinge on diverse robot interaction data, which are costly to collect. Egocentric human videos offer a complementary source of experience, and latent action models (LAMs) provide a popular means of leveraging these videos for policy supervision. Compared with world-action models (WAMs), LAMs can offer greater training efficiency and potentially lower inference costs by avoiding explicit pixel prediction during policy learning and execution. However, most existing LAMs learn latent actions solely through video reconstruction, which can cause their representations to cluster by visual appearance rather than by the underlying actions. As a result, they struggle to align human actions with their robot counterparts. To bridge the gap, we introduce SALA, which emphasizes establishing the semantic correspondence for latent actions. Without requiring paired data, we use the language descriptions of unpaired human and robot clips to estimate semantic similarities and supervise cross-embodiment correspondence. Specifically, we translate these similarities into soft neighborhood structures that guide human latent actions toward semantically related robot latents, while robot action reconstruction grounds the latent space in control. The resulting shared latent action space provides a unified supervision signal for training an embodied foundation model on both human and robot videos. Notably, latent action supervision enables scaling along two axes: (1) pre-training on increasing amounts of general human video consistently reduces robot action prediction error on downstream tasks, and (2) post-training on increasing amounts of task-specific human video substantially improves real-world robot task success rates.
bullets: Addresses the poor cross-embodiment alignment caused by learning latent actions primarily from video reconstruction.
Uses language descriptions of unpaired human and robot clips to estimate semantic similarities and create soft neighborhood supervision.
Combines cross-embodiment alignment with robot action reconstruction to ground the shared latent space in control.
Enables unified training on human and robot videos without requiring paired data.
Scaling general human video reduces downstream robot action prediction error, while task-specific human video improves real-world task success.

papers.title: SALA: Semantically Aligned Latent Actions Enable Dual-Axis Scaling of Embodied Foundation Models

papers.abstract: General-purpose language models are trained mostly on English: over open models we review, at most, non-English pretraining data makes up only a 12% share. Models built for European languages give them far more, but score well below general-purpose models of the same size. A common concern is that, in small models, languages compete for capacity. We present Lara Mini base, a model trained from scratch on 6T tokens in English and 44 other languages, which together cover all 24 official languages of the European Union. As training progresses, the 44 other languages together come to outweigh English. To give these languages enough capacity at low cost, Lara Mini base uses a mixture of experts architecture with 7.2B total and 0.6B active parameters. Among open base models with up to 2B active parameters, it achieves the highest average score across standard English, multilingual, math, and code benchmarks, ahead of models trained on 4 to 6 times as many tokens. Its margin is largest on multilingual benchmarks in the languages it supports and on math benchmarks. It supports contexts of up to 128k tokens. We find that our MoE architecture reduces capacity competition between languages. For a single user on one GPU, without quantization, it generates text at least 1.8 times faster than any model with a higher average score. We release the weights of Lara Mini base under the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license. In addition, we will release T-HellaSwag, a higher-quality machine translation of the commonsense reasoning benchmark HellaSwag into 110 language variants.

papers.abstract: We present Fikiria, a two-stage SFT+GRPO recipe for Swahili mathematical reasoning. Its reward multiplies a format gate by a weighted sum of answer accuracy and the ChrF\texttt{++} similarity of the Swahili reasoning to an in-language reference chain of thought, so that training targets the surface fidelity of the reasoning trace and not only the final answer. We train on a 2.3k-problem Swahili dataset created by translating GSM8K with GPT-4.1 and filtering with SSA-COMET. On AfriMGSM Swahili, Fikiria-AfriqueQwen-14B reaches 79.2\%. Under the same fixed prompt and strict answer-format scoring, GPT-4o reaches 68.0\%, partly because it often fails the required answer format; IrokoBench reports 78.8\% for GPT-4o using a best-per-model prompt, a figure numerically close to ours but not directly comparable. In a small human evaluation with co-author annotators, GPT-4o's outputs were preferred overall. ChrF\texttt{++} measures surface fidelity, not the validity of individual reasoning steps.
bullets: Addresses the lack of native-language Swahili mathematical reasoning training.
Uses two-stage supervised fine-tuning plus GRPO, rewarding format compliance, answer accuracy, and ChrF++ similarity to reference Swahili reasoning.
Trains on 2.3k Swahili problems translated from GSM8K and filtered with SSA-COMET.

Fikiria-AfriqueQwen-14B scores 79.2% versus 68.0% for GPT-4o under the same fixed prompt and strict scoring; the comparison is partly format-sensitive and not directly comparable to best-prompt results.
Human co-author annotators preferred GPT-4o overall, and ChrF++ does not verify the validity of individual reasoning steps.

papers.abstract: We study how to repurpose video diffusion models (VDMs), pretrained on millions of videos, for dense 3D point tracking, where training data is scarce. Doing so is non-trivial, as it requires representing 3D tracks as video-like signals that may lie outside the natural-video distribution on which the VDM was trained. We thus systematically assess the effectiveness of two such video representations. The first, Residual 3D Tracking Video (RTV), encodes per-pixel 3D offsets relative to a query frame and allows recovery of 3D trajectories directly from the generated video. The second, Normalized Coordinate Map Video (NCMV), labels each pixel with a canonical coordinate invariant through time. This is closer to a natural video and easier for the VDM to learn, but requires additional post-processing with an off-the-shelf 2D tracker to recover 3D tracks. RTV tracks more accurately, while NCMV shows that a VDM can generate dense correspondence as a video. We instantiate both representations with LoRA adaptation of a frozen Wan backbone, conditioned on point maps from an off-the-shelf 3D reconstructor as a geometric scaffold. Trained with a single dynamic 3D tracking dataset, Track4D achieves competitive zero-shot tracking on four real and synthetic benchmarks. A regression readout that bypasses the video VAE and uses additional training data brings further improvement, demonstrating the potential of this direction for dense 3D tracking. We hope our analysis will inspire future work that leverages VDM priors for dense 3D tracking and 4D reconstruction. Project page: https://nirvanalan.github.io/projects/track4d
bullets: RTV encodes per-pixel 3D offsets and directly recovers trajectories, yielding more accurate tracks.
NCMV uses time-invariant canonical coordinates, making the representation more natural for video diffusion but requiring a 2D tracker for recovery.
Both representations use LoRA adaptation of a frozen Wan backbone, guided by point maps from an off-the-shelf 3D reconstructor.
Trained on one dynamic 3D tracking dataset, Track4D achieves competitive zero-shot performance across four real and synthetic benchmarks.
A regression readout that bypasses the video VAE and uses extra training data provides further improvement.

figures.caption: Figure 2: TRACK4D overview. (a) Generative readout. A frozen reconstructor supplies point maps P; the video VAE encodes them with video V into condition C. The LoRA-adapted video DiT denoises the RTV and NCMV latents, jointly by default, and the VAE decodes the videos. Hatched targets are noised in training and start from Gaussian noise at inference. Adding inverse-normalized RTV offsets to the query-frame point map gives 3D tracks; NCMV requires 2D tracking and lifting. (b) Regression readout. Point maps enter through a patch encoder, a private motion expert attends jointly with the video DiT, and a DPT head reads residuals without the output VAE (Section 3.4 and Figure 8). Flames denote trained modules, snowflakes frozen modules.

Figure 6: TrackCraft3R vs. the three TRACK4D readouts on DAVIS [70]. Each panel shows the point cloud of frame j and the last 12 frames of the predicted 3D tracks, from one fixed view (the frame-0 input camera rotated by 4◦). All methods receive the same VGGT-Ω point maps and draw the same 767 queries, the most-moving points of a dense grid, colored by image row. papers.abstract: LLM workloads sometimes ask many independent questions about the same long document, as in document QA, data labeling and LLM-based evaluation. Prefix caching removes the redundant prefill shared by these queries, but each decode step still reads the document's key-value (KV) cache once per question, so decoding is bound by memory bandwidth and scales with the number of questions. We present Parallel Prompting, which decodes P questions as P independent streams of a single request all at once, fixing this issue. In our method, every step reads the shared document once for all P streams, and a stream-id attention mask, evaluated inside the attention kernel, keeps each answer conditioned only on the document and its own question. We implement Parallel Prompting in SGLang by adding about 80 lines to three existing files and a small engine package; the mask needs no dense tensor, and every decode step has a fixed shape that is captured as a CUDA graph. With CodeLlama-7B, 8k-16k-token documents and 64-256 questions per document, Parallel Prompting is 3.7x faster than stock SGLang with its FlashInfer backend on an A100 and 5.9-6.0x faster on an RTX A6000, on two SGLang releases, including the most recent release. Timed on identical inputs, it is faster than stock SGLang in all 144 runs (2 GPUs x 2 releases x 6 workloads x 6 input sets). Code: https://github.com/jlab-nlp/parallel-prompting
bullets: Targets document QA, labeling, and evaluation workloads with many independent questions sharing one context.

Implemented in SGLang with lightweight code changes, dense-mask-free attention, and fixed-shape CUDA graphs.
For CodeLlama-7B workloads, it achieved 3.7× speedup on an A100 and 5.9–6.0× on an RTX A6000 versus stock SGLang.
Evaluation covered 144 identical-input runs across two GPUs, two SGLang releases, six workloads, and six input sets; it was faster in every run.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Three ways to answer several questions about one document, shown at one decode step (dark: the token generated in this step). A serving engine such as SGLang or vLLM runs a batch of requests, and every decode step adds one token to each request. Batched requests with prefix caching store the document’s KV once but use one request per question, so every step reads the document once per question. Batch prompting (Cheng et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2024) puts all questions and answers in one sequence: it reads the document once, but the answers are generated one after another, and later answers attend to earlier ones. Parallel Prompting decodes the questions as streams of one request: every step adds one token per stream and reads the document once for all of them, and a stream mask (Figure 2) keeps the answers independent. The batch still has room for other requests, for example for other documents (Figure 6).

papers.abstract: We evaluate Genie Sim Benchmark through paired real-simulation tasks and complementary system-identification studies. Across 22 robot-task pairs spanning 16 task names, task-specific pi0.5 policies fine-tuned on real-robot data achieve a descriptive Score correlation of 0.9686, MAE 0.0405, RMSE 0.0520, with simulation-real differences from -0.110 to +0.080. G2 crsB experiments assess long-horizon closed-loop position and joint-side torque agreement, while five representative object cases examine identification and cross-engine contact transfer. A separate 32.6503 s teleoperation trajectory, excluded from mechanical identification and servo-gain search, evaluates external position targets through simulated motion-controller command shaping and a calibrated position servo. Across both arms, per-joint position RMSE spans 0.00614-0.03522 rad and current-derived torque RMSE spans 0.73545-4.00099 N m. Native PhysX adaptations recover three recorded interaction tasks, with case-dependent alignment gains. These results support task-specific simulation evaluation through joint assessment of task outcomes and physical-response consistency.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robotic manipulation. In our production setting, hundreds of VLA-powered robots are already operating in real-world environments, creating an immediate need for efficient fleet serving. We present XInfer, a production-deployed VLA serving system designed to reduce the inference infrastructure cost of large-scale robotic deployments. XInfer jointly coordinates heterogeneous VLA computation with the evolving response requirements of robotic execution. By exploiting computational parallelism while managing interference, XInfer improves GPU efficiency while protecting time-critical robotic feedback. We evaluate XInfer across three VLA models using production-derived workloads, achieving 1.26-3.75 times the effective robot capacity (ERC) of state-of-the-art systems under physical-execution constraints. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/X-Square-Robot/xinfer.

papers.abstract: Post-training improves language-model reasoning, but how it changes the use of internal information and verbalized chain of thought (CoT) remains unclear. We study successive SFT, DPO, and RLVR checkpoints of Olmo-3-7B-Instruct on multi-digit addition, using carry values as known intermediate state. Probes recover carry information from internal activations with similar accuracy in SFT and RLVR, although manipulating this information does not reliably control model outputs. In contrast, the usefulness of verbalized reasoning differs: CoTs produced by RLVR yield higher accuracy across receiving checkpoints than those produced by SFT or DPO. We also show that carry-related statements receive higher importance scores after RLVR than matched random controls. DPO shows similar sensitivity to carry-related statements but without comparable accuracy gains. These results suggest that post-training changes the usefulness of written reasoning and sensitivity to its content in meaningful ways, although greater sensitivity does not necessarily coincide with better problem performance.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion models provide a source of interaction representations for robot control, but transferring these representations requires reconciling variable camera inputs with heterogeneous action interfaces and closed-loop execution. We present X-World, a framework that transfers a video prior through a fixed-length token sequence to a shared action expert. A residual cross-view attention branch extends a pretrained video backbone to one, two, or three views while retaining its original self-attention path. A layer-aligned Q-Former aggregates backbone features, and dataset-specific modules map between native state and action interfaces and the shared action expert. Training separates video adaptation from action-only pretraining by freezing the video backbone in the latter stage, followed by joint target-domain post-training. The policy extracts video features with a single backbone pass and uses asynchronous action chunking for execution. On LIBERO, X-World reaches 98.5\% mean success; its LIBERO-trained checkpoint obtains 76.5\% on LIBERO-Plus without further adaptation. The seven-shift breakdown reveals gains in robot, language, lighting, and layout perturbations, alongside weaknesses under camera, background, and noise shifts relative to OpenVLA-OFT. On six dual-arm real-world tasks, it achieves 81.7\% mean success over 20 trials per task. Removing video adaptation or cross-view fusion produces the largest observed success drops among the tested removals.
bullets: Supports one, two, or three camera views using residual cross-view attention while preserving the pretrained video backbone.
Uses a fixed-length token interface, layer-aligned Q-Former, and dataset-specific state/action modules to connect heterogeneous robot interfaces to a shared action expert.
Separates video adaptation from action pretraining, then performs joint target-domain post-training; execution uses one backbone pass and asynchronous action chunking.
Reports 98.5% mean success on LIBERO, 76.5% on LIBERO-Plus without further adaptation, and 81.7% mean success across six dual-arm real-world tasks.
Shows weaknesses under camera, background, and noise shifts relative to OpenVLA-OFT; removing video adaptation or cross-view fusion causes the largest tested performance drops.

papers.abstract: Audio-visual models improve egocentric action recognition by exploiting complementary cues, yet typically assume that both streams remain available at inference. Existing missing-modality methods operate on trimmed, single-event clips in which a stream is entirely present or absent, whereas real sensors fail and recover within long, untrimmed observations. We redefine egocentric modality missingness as temporally localized sensor outages within untrimmed, multi-event observations, with whole-clip absence as the limiting case. We introduce \textbf{MacJEPA}, a missing-modality-robust \textbf{Ma}sked-\textbf{c}ontext query \textbf{JEPA} that recognizes visual actions and acoustic events from supplied interval queries over audio-visual context. Window-local modality dropout simulates these sensor outages during training. MacJEPA further repurposes masking in JEPA from a self-supervised pretext into a supervised robustness objective, aligning masked and clean latent representations of both multimodal content tokens and the task-conditioned queries. All objectives are optimized jointly with recognition in a single stage, requiring no test-time adaptation. Across Epic-Kitchens-100 and Epic-Sounds, a single checkpoint remains competitive under complete input and consistently surpasses published missing-modality baselines when either the dominant or auxiliary stream is removed. MacJEPA thus unifies strong full-input recognition with temporal missing-modality robustness in a single model operating on untrimmed multi-event videos.
bullets: Reframes missing modality as within-video, time-localized outages, including full-clip absence as a special case.
Uses a masked-context query JEPA to predict visual actions and acoustic events from interval queries over audio-visual context.
Trains with window-local modality dropout and aligns masked and clean representations for content tokens and task-conditioned queries.
Jointly optimizes robustness and recognition in one stage, without test-time adaptation.
On Epic-Kitchens-100 and Epic-Sounds, one checkpoint remains competitive with full input and outperforms published missing-modality baselines when either stream is removed.

papers.abstract: Recent video world models have witnessed the paradigm shift from single-agent to multi-agent involvements, which can reveal more complicated dynamics and cross-agent interaction in the real world. However, existing approaches commonly adopt implicit inter-agent communications via cross attention, which lack explicit geometry constraints and unified 3D state, thereby leading to poor multi-view consistency and struggling with recovering out-of-sight agents. In addition, most of them assume a static background, failing to represent uncontrolled background dynamics. To address these problems, we propose Artemis: a geometry-grounded multi-agent world model with explicit memory sharing. An explicit 3D world map is reconstructed from multi-agent observations to enforce a unified 3D state across agents, offering high cross-view consistency. Specifically, an action-guided geometric injection module is developed to simultaneously render decomposed foreground-background control maps, which are then injected into a diffusion transformer through a designed GeoAdapter block. Compared to previous methods assuming static-only background, our GeoAdapter can also distinguish uncontrolled non-agent dynamics, which are conditioned on their own multi-frame history positions to provide consistent motion cues. Keyframes selected from progressive video rollouts are used to progressively update the reconstructed 3D world maps. To effectively capture complex dynamic patterns, we curate a novel dataset sampled from the CARLA simulator called MA-CARLA. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method in terms of visual fidelity and cross-view consistency in the generated videos. In addition, our Artemis can support simultaneous multi-modal rollouts with both 2D video and 3D point map maintenance, scale to scenarios beyond two agents and multi-camera setting.
bullets: Addresses poor cross-view consistency, out-of-sight agent recovery, and static-background assumptions in prior multi-agent world models.
Reconstructs an explicit 3D world map from multi-agent observations to enforce a unified geometric state.

Models uncontrolled background dynamics using their own multi-frame position histories, while keyframes progressively update the 3D map.
Introduces the MA-CARLA dataset; experiments report improved visual fidelity and cross-view consistency, with support for multi-modal 2D video/3D point-map rollouts and more than two agents.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based world models can generate and predict trajectories in high-dimensional dynamical systems, but predictive accuracy does not imply that their latent coordinates recover the underlying state variables or causal interactions. We ask whether a frozen pretrained diffusion model can be equipped with identifiable coordinates without retraining its generative backbone. We show that auxiliary-variable nonlinear ICA guarantees can be transferred to Contrastive Diffusion Alignment (ConDA), which learns only a lightweight alignment map on top of frozen diffusion latents. Under standard TCL/GCL assumptions, the aligned representation identifies latent dynamical states up to permutation and componentwise invertible transformations, preserves the latent dynamic structural causal model, and reduces lagged graph recovery to transition-Jacobian sparsity. We evaluate TCL-, GCL-, and CEBRA-based ConDA against TDRL, CaRiNG, IDOL, temporal SuaVE, and iVAE across physical and robotic video systems. TCL and GCL achieve near-perfect blockwise state recovery and competitive lagged graph recovery, including exact recovery in a simulated falling-body system. In a simulated bipedal robot, learned dynamics recover the sign and temporal structure of responses to held-out control perturbations. These results show that a frozen generative diffusion model can be equipped with coordinates that are identifiable, structurally interpretable, and useful for analyzing intervention-relevant dynamics.
bullets: Addresses the gap between accurate trajectory prediction and recovery of true latent state variables or causal structure.
Applies auxiliary-variable nonlinear ICA guarantees to Contrastive Diffusion Alignment (ConDA) without retraining the diffusion backbone.
Under TCL/GCL assumptions, states are identified up to permutation and componentwise invertible transformations, while latent structural dynamics are preserved.
Experiments on physical and robotic video systems show near-perfect blockwise state recovery, competitive lagged graph recovery, and exact recovery in a simulated falling-body system.
Control-perturbation tests in a simulated bipedal robot recover the sign and temporal structure of held-out responses.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the proposed framework. (a) A frozen pretrained diffusion model serves as a generative world model: it embeds video frames yt into diffusion latents xt by inversion (solid arrows) and decodes latents back into frames (dashed arrows). The latents are in turn generated by a lagged dynamic SCM over the latent state st, driven by inputs ut and independent noise, through xt = g(st). (b) TCL- or GCL-based ConDA trains only a lightweight map h, using temporal or auxiliary information, to obtain zt = h(xt). Under nonlinear ICA assumptions, zt identifies st up to permutation and componentwise invertible transformations, and can be lifted back to xt for generation. (c) Lagged causal structure is characterized theoretically by inverse transition-noise Jacobian sparsity and estimated empirically from states aligned from zt. Dynamics learned in these coordinates are validated by predicting responses to held-out control perturbations.

Figure 2: Recovered lag-1 dynamics graphs across datasets and methods. Binary adjacency matrices are shown for IDOL, CaRiNG, TDRL, temporal SuaVE, iVAE, ConDA-CEBRA, ConDATCL, ConDA-GCL, and the true-state reference. Blue entries indicate recovered edges and gray entries indicate absent edges. Rows correspond to the different dynamical systems considered in the study. The ConDA variants more closely reproduce the sparsity structure of the true-state dynamics, with TCL and GCL showing particularly strong agreement across settings.

The curves compare the MuJoCo simulator response, the true-state dynamics baseline, and the TCL-aligned representation. papers.abstract: The key-value (KV) cache of autoregressive transformers grows linearly with context length and dominates memory at long context. Most training-free remedies evict low-importance tokens, an irreversible choice along the sequence axis. We instead keep every token and store it more cheaply along the "feature" axis. We therefore propose AttSVD, a new "interpretable" low-rank compression whose basis is derived from each prompt's own attention geometry: an online, per-prompt truncated SVD that keeps only the directions attention actually reads, cutting persistent per-head KV memory in proportion to the retained rank. We propose two decode-time caching strategies, accumulating and streaming, for short and long generation regimes. Furthermore, we propose two refinements that make compression adaptive. A per-matrix energy rule sizes the logit space and the attention mass independently. An attention-aware basis truncates only in the spaces attention actually reads, preserving both the attention logits and the attention output. The same factors also provide free, per-head interpretability insights into the effective rank and the geometry attention consumes. Across multiple models, on both an agentic benchmark and the full LongBench suite AttSVD stays on par with the dense cache while using up to 50% of the KV-cache memory.
bullets: Addresses the linear KV-cache memory growth of long-context autoregressive transformers without evicting tokens.
Derives an online, per-prompt SVD basis from attention geometry and retains only attention-relevant feature directions.
Introduces accumulating and streaming decode-time caching strategies for short- and long-generation settings.
Uses independent energy-based rank selection and attention-aware truncation to preserve attention logits and outputs.
Matches dense-cache performance across multiple models, an agentic benchmark, and LongBench, with up to 50% KV-memory reduction.
